# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The benchmark focuses on disordered binary optimization problems whose objective
function can be interpreted as an energy landscape. The basic task is simple to
state: given a set of binary variables and a set of random interactions or
constraints, find an assignment that minimizes the total energy. The difficulty
comes from the structure of the landscape. In frustrated systems, local
preferences cannot all be satisfied at the same time. As the system size grows,
this produces many competing low-energy configurations, metastable minima, and
barriers separating different regions of configuration space. This is the
physical mechanism behind the use of spin glasses as paradigmatic hard
optimization problems [@sherrington1975; @edwards1975; @mezard1987].

Spin-glass and XORSAT instances are useful benchmarks because they combine
hardness with theoretical control. Some variants are NP-hard in the worst case,
while others admit exact algorithms or exact asymptotic results in selected
limits [@barahona1982; @lucas2014; @talagrand2006]. This makes the family richer
than a generic collection of hard instances: one can compare worst-case and
typical-case behaviour, use small or exactly solvable instances for validation,
and then increase the size or change the topology to enter regimes where generic
heuristics struggle. A small instance may be solved by enumeration, exact solvers,
or simple local search; the same ensemble at larger sizes can display much more
severe glassy behaviour.

The theoretical motivation is rooted in the Parisi solution of the
Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model and in the broader statistical-physics description
of random optimization and constraint-satisfaction problems. In this view,
hardness is not only a matter of the best possible algorithm, but also of the
organization of states: clustering of solutions, overlap structure, replica
symmetry breaking, and energetic or entropic barriers [@parisi1979; @parisi1980;
@mezard1987; @mezard2009; @krzakala2007]. These concepts are useful when building
benchmarks because they provide language for explaining *why* an instance is
hard, not only whether a solver succeeds or fails.

For this reason, spin glasses and XORSAT have been used across several domains as
test beds for optimization algorithms. They appear in classical simulated
annealing and related Monte Carlo methods, quantum annealing and adiabatic
optimization, QAOA and gate-based variational algorithms, quantum-inspired
methods, and recent AI/ML-assisted solvers [@kirkpatrick1983sa; @kadowaki1998;
@santoro2002; @albash2018; @bapst2013; @farhi2014qaoa; @boettcher2023;
@schuetz2022gnn; @biazzo2024; @biazzo2023autoregressive; @delbono2025; @delbono2026]. The benchmark therefore uses these
problems not as an abstract physics exercise, but as a common controlled ground
on which classical, AI-based, quantum-inspired, and quantum optimization
approaches can be compared.

The current scope contains two main classes of problems:

1. **pairwise Ising spin glasses**, where the variables are spins
   $s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ and the objective is a quadratic energy;
2. **XORSAT-type constraint-satisfaction problems**, which are naturally
   higher-order parity problems but can also be reduced to pairwise Ising or QUBO
   form when required by a solver.

The following sections define these problems and explain the role played by each
family in the benchmark.

# Spin-glass optimization problems {#sec-spin-glass}

## General Ising spin-glass formulation {#sec-ising-general}

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph with $N=|V|$ vertices. Each vertex carries an Ising spin
$s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$. Given pairwise couplings $J_{ij}$ on the edges and,
optionally, local fields $h_i$, the general Ising optimization problem is

$$
H(\mathbf{s})
= - \sum_{(i,j)\in E} J_{ij} s_i s_j
  - \sum_{i\in V} h_i s_i .
$$

The optimization task is to find

$$
\mathbf{s}^{\star} \in \arg\min_{\mathbf{s}\in\{-1,+1\}^{N}} H(\mathbf{s}) .
$$

Positive couplings favour aligned spins, while negative couplings favour
anti-aligned spins. On graphs with loops, these local preferences can be mutually
inconsistent. The resulting frustration is what produces a rugged energy
landscape with many local minima.

This formulation is closely related to Quadratic Unconstrained Binary
Optimization (QUBO). By changing variables between spins $s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ and
bits $x_i \in \{0,1\}$, for example through $s_i = 2x_i-1$, a pairwise Ising
energy can be written as a quadratic polynomial in binary variables
[@glover2019qubo; @lucas2014]. This connection is important because different
classical and quantum solvers use different native representations: some expect
Ising couplings, while others expect QUBO coefficients.

In the repository, the main distinction among spin-glass families is the graph
$G$: complete graph for the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model, finite-dimensional
lattices for the Edwards--Anderson model, and sparse random graphs for random
regular graph spin glasses.

## Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model {#sec-sk}

### Definition

The Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model is the fully connected mean-field Ising
spin glass. Every spin interacts with every other spin. A standard zero-field
form is

$$
H_{\mathrm{SK}}(\mathbf{s})
= - \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}
  \sum_{1\le i<j\le N} J_{ij} s_i s_j,
$$

where the couplings $J_{ij}$ are independent random variables, commonly Gaussian
with zero mean and unit variance or bimodal $J_{ij}\in\{-1,+1\}$. The factor
$1/\sqrt{N}$ gives an extensive thermodynamic normalization [@sherrington1975].

### Why it is included

SK is the canonical dense spin-glass benchmark. It is mathematically central
because the thermodynamic solution is described by Parisi's replica-symmetry
breaking construction [@parisi1979; @parisi1980; @mezard1987], and the limiting
free energy is rigorously characterized by the Parisi formula [@talagrand2006].
This gives the model an unusually strong theoretical status: it is hard, but not
unstructured.

From a benchmarking point of view, SK tests how a solver deals with dense,
long-range interactions. 

### What it tests

SK is useful for testing:

- dense all-to-all connectivity;
- behaviour on mean-field glassy landscapes;
- finite-size convergence toward known asymptotic quantities;
- algorithms designed for dense QUBO or dense Ising problems;
- embedding and routing overhead on hardware with sparse native connectivity.

Its main limitation is also its strength: because the graph is complete, it is
not native to most near-term quantum hardware. Therefore, when SK is used on
sparse hardware, one must distinguish algorithmic difficulty from the overhead of
embedding a dense graph into a sparse device topology.

## Edwards--Anderson model {#sec-ea}

### Definition

The Edwards--Anderson (EA) model is a finite-dimensional spin glass. Spins live
on the sites of a $d$-dimensional lattice and interact only with nearest
neighbours:

$$
H_{\mathrm{EA}}(\mathbf{s})
= - \sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} J_{ij} s_i s_j .
$$

Here $\langle i,j\rangle$ denotes nearest-neighbour lattice edges, and the
couplings are usually drawn from either a Gaussian or bimodal distribution
[@edwards1975]. The lattice may have open or periodic boundary conditions,
depending on the intended benchmark use.

### Two-dimensional EA

The two-dimensional zero-field EA model plays a special role. For planar
instances without magnetic fields, exact ground states can be found in polynomial
time using mappings to matching problems [@barahona1982]. This means that 2D EA
can be used as a controlled validation family: heuristic solvers can be tested
against certified optima at sizes much larger than those accessible by brute
force.

This does not make 2D EA useless as a benchmark. Rather, it gives it a precise
role. It is especially useful for calibration, finite-size studies, and tests in
which one wants a local spin-glass landscape but also wants access to exact
answers.

### Three-dimensional EA

The three-dimensional EA model is much harder. Moving from two to three spatial
dimensions removes the planar structure that makes the zero-field 2D case
tractable, and the ground-state problem becomes NP-hard [@barahona1982]. The 3D
model is therefore a natural finite-dimensional hard benchmark: it preserves
local interactions and geometric structure, but it is no longer an exactly
solvable validation case.

### Why it is included

EA models are included because they provide the finite-dimensional and local
counterpart to SK. They allow the benchmark to separate dense mean-field hardness
from local geometric hardness. In particular:

- 2D EA provides local spin-glass instances with exact ground truth in selected
  settings;
- 3D EA provides a genuinely hard finite-dimensional spin-glass benchmark;
- both variants are closer to physical hardware connectivity than SK;
- comparing 2D and 3D EA makes it possible to study how dimensionality changes
  algorithmic behaviour.

## Spin glasses on sparse random graphs {#sec-rrg}

### Definition

Sparse random-graph spin glasses place pairwise Ising interactions on random
sparse graphs rather than on a lattice or on the complete graph. Given a graph
$G=(V,E)$, the Hamiltonian is

$$
H_G(\mathbf{s})
= - \sum_{(i,j)\in E} J_{ij} s_i s_j .
$$

The main sparse graph ensemble used in the benchmark is the random regular graph
(RRG). In a $c$-regular graph, every vertex has exactly $c$ neighbours. Couplings
may again be Gaussian or bimodal. Erdős--Rényi graphs with fixed average degree
can also be considered, but RRG instances are often cleaner because the degree is
controlled exactly.

### Why random regular graphs are useful

Random regular graphs sit between SK and EA. Like SK, they are random and have a
mean-field character. Like EA, they have finite degree and therefore sparse
connectivity. Locally, large random regular graphs are tree-like, which connects
them to the cavity method and to the statistical physics of random
constraint-satisfaction problems [@mezard2009].

This makes RRG spin glasses useful for studying typical-case hardness. They are
less geometrically structured than lattices, but they do not have the dense
all-to-all structure of SK. The connectivity $c$ is also a natural control
parameter: by changing $c$, one changes the local degree, the density of
constraints, and the cost of embedding the problem on sparse hardware.

### What they test

Sparse random-graph spin glasses are useful for testing:

- finite-connectivity mean-field behaviour;
- typical-case hardness on random sparse structures;
- message-passing, graph-based, and local algorithms;
- QAOA and other algorithms whose performance depends strongly on graph locality;
- the transition between lattice-like sparse problems and dense mean-field
  problems.

For the benchmark, these instances are particularly important because they are
scalable and tunable while remaining conceptually close to spin-glass theory.

# XORSAT optimization problems {#sec-xorsat}

## General XORSAT formulation {#sec-xorsat-general}

An XORSAT instance is a system of parity constraints over binary variables
$x_i\in\{0,1\}$. In 3-XORSAT, each constraint involves three variables:

$$
x_{i_a} \oplus x_{j_a} \oplus x_{k_a} = b_a,
\qquad a=1,\ldots,M,
$$

where $b_a\in\{0,1\}$ and $\oplus$ denotes addition modulo two. The native problem
is linear over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$, and therefore satisfiable instances can be
solved algebraically by Gaussian elimination. This algebraic solvability is one
reason XORSAT is useful as a benchmark: it allows one to know or plant solutions
while still creating instances that are difficult for generic optimization
heuristics [@hen2019; @kowalsky2022].

## Spin formulation of 3-XORSAT {#sec-xorsat-spin}

Using spin variables

$$
s_i = (-1)^{x_i},
\qquad
J_a = (-1)^{b_a},
$$

a parity constraint is satisfied when

$$
J_a s_{i_a}s_{j_a}s_{k_a} = 1 .
$$

A natural cost function is therefore

$$
H_{\mathrm{3X}}(\mathbf{s})
= \sum_{a=1}^{M}
  \frac{1 - J_a s_{i_a}s_{j_a}s_{k_a}}{2} .
$$

This energy counts the number of violated clauses. The global minimum is zero
for satisfiable instances and positive for unsatisfiable instances.

The important difference from the pairwise spin glasses above is that this is a
three-body Hamiltonian. Each term couples three spins, not two. This makes XORSAT
a natural benchmark for higher-order optimization, while also raising an encoding
question for solvers that only accept pairwise Ising or QUBO inputs.

## Planted and regular XORSAT instances {#sec-xorsat-planted}

The benchmark should include planted or regular variants of XORSAT. In a planted
instance, a solution is chosen first and the clauses are generated so that this
solution satisfies them. In a regular instance, each variable appears in a fixed
number of clauses. These choices make the ensemble controlled and reproducible,
and they allow the optimum to be known by construction [@hen2019; @kowalsky2022].

XORSAT is especially useful because it separates algebraic solvability from
heuristic optimization difficulty. A solver that recognizes the linear structure
can solve the instance efficiently, but a generic local-search, annealing, or
black-box optimization method may experience a difficult landscape. In regular
and planted ensembles, the hard regime is often associated with isolated clusters
of solutions and entropic barriers: the challenge is not simply to cross a high
energy wall, but to find a small target region in a very large configuration
space [@mezard2002; @krzakala2007; @bellitti2021; @bernaschi2021xorsat].

## Pairwise Ising and QUBO reductions {#sec-xorsat-qubo}

Many optimization solvers, especially hardware solvers, accept only pairwise
Ising or QUBO formulations. For this reason, the benchmark should document two
representations of XORSAT instances:

1. the **native clause representation**, which preserves the original parity
   constraints;
2. the **encoded pairwise representation**, where auxiliary variables and penalty
   terms reduce the three-body interactions to quadratic form.

The native representation is the cleanest mathematical definition. The encoded
representation is the one needed for pairwise Ising/QUBO solvers. Both are useful,
but they should not be confused: the encoding introduces additional variables,
penalty scales, and possible changes in the effective landscape. These overheads
are part of what the benchmark should make explicit.

# Summary of benchmark roles {#sec-summary}

| Family | Topology | Native interaction | Main benchmark role |
|---|---|---|---|
| SK | Complete graph | Pairwise Ising | Dense mean-field spin glass with strong theoretical control |
| EA 2D | Two-dimensional lattice | Pairwise Ising | Local spin glass with exact ground truth in selected zero-field planar cases |
| EA 3D | Three-dimensional lattice | Pairwise Ising | Hard finite-dimensional local spin-glass benchmark |
| RRG spin glass | Sparse random regular graph | Pairwise Ising | Finite-connectivity mean-field benchmark with tunable degree |
| 3-XORSAT | Random or planted hypergraph | Three-body parity constraints | Constraint-satisfaction benchmark with known/planted solutions and entropic hardness |

The benchmark is therefore not based on a single notion of hardness. SK tests
dense mean-field glassiness; EA tests finite-dimensional locality; RRG spin
glasses test sparse random typical-case behaviour; and XORSAT tests structured
constraint satisfaction, higher-order interactions, and planted hardness. Taken
together, these families provide a compact but expressive set of problems for
comparing classical, AI/ML-based, quantum-inspired, and quantum optimization
methods.
